items.title: Is the AI Bubble Popping?
items.description:
Recorded November 5, 2026.

Last Thursday, Alphabet, Google's parent company, lost nearly $500 billion in a single day, its worst day since it went public in 2004. A week later, on November 5, AI stocks fell together and the Nasdaq slid into a correction. So is the AI bubble popping?

In this episode I measure the sell-off against the line one big study uses for a crash, look at what Big Tech is spending on AI and what companies say they're getting back, compare it with the dot-com crash, and hold chip stocks up to the warning signs that came before past crashes. Then I tell you what I think it means for your retirement account and your career.

So what do you think? Is the AI bubble popping, or is this just a bad few weeks? Leave me your thoughts in the comments.

Chapters
0:00 Two big drops
0:54 What a pop looks like
1:29 How far we've fallen
2:06 Why investors are spooked
3:45 The last time a bubble popped
4:36 Will it keep going?
5:39 What it means for you
6:20 My answer

More from me: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC-N6X4gJtGrTDSAuOea8nEA · Instagram https://www.instagram.com/davidpark_phd/

The narration in this video is an AI-generated version of David Park's own voice, made from his recordings.

This video is for education, not investment advice. Prices are daily closes as of November 5, 2026. The firm survey is a working paper, not yet published in a journal; the "about half" crash figure is from the study's working-paper version (NBER w23191).

items.title: Should We Shut Down Business Schools?
items.description:
Should we shut down business schools? Christopher Marquis, a professor who has taught at Harvard Business School, Cornell and Cambridge, argued in The New York Times that we should. I teach at a business school myself, so I've got skin in this game.

In this episode I lay out his case: students who arrive wanting to bring clean energy to market and leave chasing consulting and finance jobs, Harvard cases that praised Enron, and a study that found pay fell at companies that switched to a CEO with a business degree. Then I give you my three reasons for disagreeing, and where I think he's right.

So what do you think? Should we shut down business schools, or fix them? Tell me in the comments.

items.title: Is AI Killing the PhD?
items.description:
Recorded November 7, 2026.

This year, nearly three in ten science and engineering PhD dissertations at American universities contain writing that an AI produced. Back in 2023, it was fewer than two in a hundred. So is AI killing the PhD?

In this episode I look at the new NBER study behind that number; at the Google AI system whose top idea matched, in about two days, the answer an Imperial College lab spent about ten years on; and at a test where today's best AI models outscore PhD experts. Then I look at why universities are actually closing PhD seats this year, and I tell you which part of the PhD I think AI is killing, and which part is worth more now.

Related episode, the money side of AI: Is the AI Bubble Popping? https://youtu.be/aCgom-OUEHE

Here's my question for you. Say a student lets AI write most of the dissertation, but the discovery in it is theirs and they ran every experiment. Did they earn the PhD? Yes or no, and give me your best reason in the comments.

Chapters
0:00 Three in ten dissertations
0:59 The case for yes
2:17 Why PhD seats are closing
3:04 What AI is actually doing
4:27 What the AI didn't do
4:59 My answer
5:37 What it means for you
6:05 The number nobody has yet

More from me: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC-N6X4gJtGrTDSAuOea8nEA · Instagram https://www.instagram.com/davidpark_phd/

The narration in this video is an AI-generated version of David Park's own voice, made from his recordings.

The NBER study is a working paper, not yet peer reviewed. It ran an AI detector over dissertation abstracts, so it measures AI-written summaries, not who did the thinking. The typeset dissertation page in this video is made up for illustration. The red marks on the wall of real dissertation pages are random and say nothing about any thesis.

items.title: Nvidia Just Lost Jensen Huang. Now What?
items.description:
Recorded November 12, 2026.

Jensen Huang ran Nvidia for 33 years. A few days after he told his staff "I was unfaithful to my wife," he resigned as CEO and as a director. Reports say the woman worked for one of Nvidia's biggest customers, and that US officials believe she's a Chinese spy. So Nvidia just lost the only CEO it has ever had. Now what?

Watch next: Is AI Killing the PhD? https://youtu.be/EFDX_sdvqzc

I walk through what happened day by day, what investors call key-person risk (I call it owner risk), and what Nvidia's and Tesla's filings say about it. Then I compare Nvidia's fall with Intel in 2018 and McDonald's in 2019. My read: Intel and McDonald's lost a manager, and Nvidia lost its founder.

The choice I can't settle: make Colette Kress the permanent CEO, with no learning curve but built Huang's way, or bring in an outsider who could build the bench Huang never did, but would have to learn Nvidia with the whole market watching. Which do you pick, and what's the one reason that tips it?

Chapters
0:00 Nvidia just lost Jensen Huang
0:50 What happened
2:35 What owner risk is
3:27 Musk, the version written down
4:15 Nvidia, the version not written down
5:11 Compared to what?
6:18 My answer
7:13 What it means for you
8:09 Your seat on the board

More from me: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC-N6X4gJtGrTDSAuOea8nEA · Instagram https://www.instagram.com/davidpark_phd/

The narration in this video is an AI-generated version of David Park's own voice, made from his recordings.

The spy claims are reports, not proven; no charges have been reported, and China denies them. Huang resigned; the board accepted his resignation after reports that it was preparing to force him out. Stock moves are close-to-close from Yahoo Finance; the week runs from the Nov 6 close ($186.64) to the Nov 12 close ($166.19). Market values use 24.1 billion shares (Nvidia 10-Q, August 2026). The Intel and McDonald's figures are one-day moves; the study's figure is the average market reaction when the accused was the CEO, as reported by its authors.
